whatItFakes: A relative or acquaintance living elsewhere (the inactive tier) never moves into the played town: their move skips a relative or county destination that is one of the town's full-detail places and goes to the next record instead.
why: A husk in town would sit outside the town's residents, counts and voter rolls; arriving needs the counted arrival path or a fill-in, which the two-level population allows only when the player meets them.
replacement: A husk whose move lands in the played town arrives through the counted-moves arrival path as one counted household (one model, two tiers), filled in when the player meets them.

whatItFakes: A relative or town leaver living elsewhere works, is let go, finds work and moves to another job with no employer named: the world keeps no firms outside the played town.
why: Firms exist only for the played town's businesses; a second economy of named employers elsewhere would be a second engine.
replacement: The regional engine's employers by industry for each state (counted, never named until met) give a person living elsewhere an employer record their work spell names, filled in when the player meets it.

whatItFakes: Someone living elsewhere who was out of the labor force on day one (a student, a parent at home, someone not looking) stays out until they reach the age of retiring.
why: The pre-start run's pulls are for people in the labor force; entering it (school's end, a youngest child's age, a partner's lost job) needs its causes for people with no school or household records.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The jobs engine's enter choice (the one counted and full people make) read for people living elsewhere from their age, household and partner's work, checked against CPS flows into the labor force by age.

whatItFakes: A partner met by someone living elsewhere is always of the other sex: no adult carries a recorded orientation, so the pairing cannot read one (owner, Oct 19: "who pairs with whom reads each person's own record, including orientation"; #4963's woman-and-man pairing was ruled a defect).
why: The partnership chain's rates are by sex and the spouse age gap is for opposite-sex couples (CPS FG3); same-sex couples need their own share and age gap.
replacement: people-orientation-record: every adult carries a recorded orientation, and the partner met is of a sex both records admit, with the ACS share of same-sex couples (about 1.5%) and their age gaps checking totals.

whatItFakes: A partnership formed for someone living elsewhere, or a partner from the wider population met by a single in the played town, is recorded straight as a marriage (union: married) at line 394; the town's own couples now climb dating, living together, engaged and married, but the elsewhere tier has no cohabiting stage.
why: The partnership chain holds marriage paces only (ACS, NCFMR, NSFG first marriages); cohabitation needs its own entry and dissolution paces.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: NSFG cohabitation and transition-to-marriage paces by age, so a union starts as cohabiting or married and a cohabitation marries or ends at its own pace.

whatItFakes: A couple in the played town climbs dating, living together, engaged and married on set stage lengths (partnerDatingMonths, partnerLivingTogetherMonths, partnerEngagedMonths), tuned by a builder not sourced, moved by the pair's traits; a single whose pull is full and who knows nobody fitting meets a partner from the wider population who already shares their home.
why: The chain holds union paces only; there is no sourced pace for how long a dating couple waits to move in or to marry, nor for dating couples ending at their own rate.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: NSFG/ACS transition paces by age and union duration (dating to living together, living together to marrying or ending), and the meetings engine bringing singles together so a fitting partner is known before the pull is full.

whatItFakes: The counted population's household types never change by partnering or parting.
why: One model, two tiers (CTO, Nov 1): the counted groups should partner and part by the same yearly paces times their count, moving the household-type counts.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: people-partnership-counted (with its parts people-partnership-counted-leave-home and people-partnership-counted-pair-and-split): the counted households partner and part by partneringPerYear and separatingPerYear times their count, merging and splitting counted households.

whatItFakes: Relatives elsewhere write in proportion to closeness alone; the writer's traits (a letter writer or not) do not move how often.
why: No decision row for staying in touch exists in data/content/trait-decisions.json; the people engine's contact-known-person action reaches only town residents.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A trait-decision row for keeping in touch with a relative elsewhere, weighed against the month's typical like the partnering pull.

whatItFakes: A new hire's mentor is the eldest coworker at least mentorAgeGapYears older; the pair's traits, the work they share and whether the mentor wants to are not weighed. Hires are read from jobs the monthly review has not seen, since the jobs engine writes no hire record. The code carries no stopgap marker call (only parameters.json cites the id).
why: No mentorship or hire event exists in the new core; the jobs engine records a hire only as the job itself.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A hire event from the jobs engine, and a trait decision for taking someone on, weighed against the month's typical.

whatItFakes: Every serious illness onset is treated as a sudden episode a housemate meets; slow illnesses (a diagnosis after months) are not told apart, and a visitor or a stranger present is not considered.
why: The health engine's onset record carries no acuity or place of onset.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An acuity and a place on the health onset record (condition rows), so only sudden episodes are rescued, by whoever is present there.

whatItFakes: Every missed loan payment is a quarrel with the closest grown housemate, the borrower owing the apology; the pair's traits, who earns what and whether the money was shared are not weighed, and quarrels over anything but money are not written.
why: No dispute record exists in the new core; the missed payment is the one money trouble that names a household's member.
replacement: A dispute engine weighing the pair's traits, shared money and the household's strain, with quarrels over rules and belief as well as money.

whatItFakes: People arriving from abroad come at each state's sourced yearly rate (ACS B07001 line 081) times its people, in the nation's age mix, and settle among the counted places in proportion to who lives there. The size of the flow does not respond to a place's own pull (jobs, rents, wages), so a booming state draws no more than a slack one.
why: The sourced rate sizes the outside flow (owner, Nov 8: real rates are not targets, so it is a size, never a refit target); a pull-weighted destination needs the same pull model as the between-state moves applied to arrivals from abroad, which this change did not build.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Weigh the abroad flow's destination by the same pull the between-state moves use (wages, jobs, prices), scaled from the sourced national size so a place's own conditions draw more or fewer newcomers; the within-US gravity fit is not applied to it.

whatItFakes: A household's origin (white, Hispanic, Black, Asian, other) is drawn from the state's adult shares by race and Hispanic origin (CPS 2024, table 4b), not the town's own, and every member of a household, a couple included, shares one origin; kin take a resident relative's.
why: The repository holds only the state-level survey table; the town's own shares need the ACS place table (a Census key), and mixed couples need a joint distribution.
replacement: ACS B03002 shares for the town's place (and county for kin), and mixed-origin couples from the ACS joint table, so a child's origin comes from both parents.

whatItFakes: The county's sampled working adults carry a county employer (a sector group of the county's Census County Business Patterns employment, in workgroups of openingCoworkerGroupSize) as a household record, not a job at a modeled organization: they have no wage flow, payroll or job record, and a filled-in county person has no job.
why: A real county employer needs an organization, payroll calendar and cash in the business engine for every county firm; the county outside the town is only sampled, so the sector group stands for the workgroup candidacy's standing reads.
replacement: County employers as organizations the business and jobs engines run coarsely (recorded establishments by size class from County Business Patterns), with pay from the county's ACS earnings, so a filled-in county worker holds a real job.

whatItFakes: No one holds a civic role (a board seat, the party committee, the volunteer fire department) at the opening: the `civicRoles` field exists on every person and counted member but is never written, and party activity is one national share for every county.
why: The repository holds no list of a place's boards, committees or volunteer departments with their members, and no county share of party activity.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Roles from the place's own records where they exist (the municipal governance and special-district data), and a county share of party activity from state party-registration counts.

whatItFakes: A relative living elsewhere has their whole past read against the place they live in when their card is first opened. One who moved in play before the player opened them is schooled and worked where they live now, not where they lived on the opening day.
why: The moves engine keeps a relative's moves in play as events, and the past's one reader of where someone lived (residenceOn) reads only the moves before the start.
replacement: residenceOn reads a relative's moves in play as well, so their past is read against the place they lived on the opening day whenever they are opened.
